chunks.text: 2.1 Explainability and counterfactual model probing Many post-hoc image explanations assign importance to pixels or regions. Their reliability depends on whether the explanation actually changes with the learned model, a point made explicit by saliency-map sanity checks [ 1 ] and by work on explainability in precision pathology [ 21 ] . Counterfactual explanations take a different form: they search for a nearby input with a different prediction. Goyal et al . use discriminative visual comparisons [ 10 ] . DVCE and DiME place classifier-guided edits under diffusion image priors [ 3 , 18 ] , and DiG-IN extends diffusion guidance to comparisons between networks and neuron-level visualization [ 4 ] . Interventions have also been used to examine the generative model itself. Tinaz et al . fit sparse autoencoders to diffusion activations, identify concepts at different denoising stages, and manipulate image composition and style through those concepts [ 35 ] . This line of work is useful for understanding where a generative representation forms. Our experiments instead use a conditional generator as an input instrument for testing external pathology models. Histopathology counterfactual methods include synthetic class transitions linked to molecular labels [ 8 ] and MoPaDi, which couples a diffusion autoencoder [ 27 ] to classifiers and multiple-instance models to edit morphology toward a target prediction [ 43 ] . These approaches motivate biologically plausible edits. Our evaluation additionally requires the requested intervention to be recovered from the generated image before that image is used for model probing. 3 Method 3.1 Framework overview CPathOGen is an interventional image-synthesis framework for examining how computational pathology models respond to controlled changes in H&E input tiles.

Figure 1 presents the overall use case: a control is modified, CPathOGen generates a matched H&E counterfactual, and the response of a frozen downstream model is recorded for model interpretation. Figure 2 summarizes the construction of the conditional generator. During training, CellViT++ extracts weak cellular labels from real H&E tiles. These labels are converted into a cellular spatial map and a global morphology/appearance vector, which condition a Stable Diffusion 2.1 latent-diffusion model through latent spatial conditioning and blockwise FiLM. At inference, the same condition format can be extracted from a real tile, manually modified, or constructed by the user. 3.2 Weakly supervised condition construction As illustrated on the left of Figure 2 , to construct conditions for generator training at scale, we use pretrained nucleus segmentation and cell-classification models. In our implementation, CellViT++ provides nucleus contours, centroids, and predicted cell types. These predictions are treated as weak labels rather than manual ground truth. Let an analyzer 𝒜 \mathcal{A} applied to an H&E tile x x produce 𝒜 ⁡ ( x ) = { ( 𝐪 n , y n , ω n ) } n = 1 N , \mathcal{A}(x)=\left\{(\mathbf{q}_{n},y_{n},\omega_{n})\right\}_{n=1}^{N}, (1) where N N is the number of detected nuclei, 𝐪 n \mathbf{q}_{n} is the centroid of nucleus n n , y n y_{n} is its predicted cellular compartment, and ω n \omega_{n} is its instance contour. The spatial condition is represented by S ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] K × H × W S\in[0,1]^{K\times H\times W} , where K K is the number of cellular compartments and H H and W W are the tile height and width.

Each channel is constructed by rasterizing the centroids belonging to one cellular compartment: S k ( 𝐮 ) = Norm [ ∑ n : y n = k κ ( 𝐮 − 𝐪 n ) ] , S_{k}(\mathbf{u})=\operatorname{Norm}\left[\sum_{n:y_{n}=k}\kappa(\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{q}_{n})\right], (2) where 𝐮 \mathbf{u} denotes a pixel location, κ \kappa is a localized spatial kernel, and Norm \operatorname{Norm} scales the resulting channel to a common range. We use K = 5 K=5 channels corresponding to tumor, inflammatory, epithelial, stromal, and necrotic compartments. A global morphology and appearance condition m ∈ ℝ d m\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is computed from the detected nucleus contours and corresponding image regions: m = Std ⁡ [ Φ ⁡ ( x , 𝒜 ⁡ ( x ) ) ] , m=\operatorname{Std}\left[\Phi\bigl(x,\mathcal{A}(x)\bigr)\right], (3) where Φ \Phi aggregates the mean and dispersion of nuclear size, perimeter, eccentricity, solidity, nuclear gradient, and RGB appearance statistics. The operator Std \operatorname{Std} applies the feature-wise standardization used during model training. Our implementation uses d = 16 d=16 features. The preprocessing parameters, feature ordering, and supported control ranges are stored with the model and reused during inference. This is particularly important for the appearance dimensions, for which incorrect standardization or feature ordering can produce globally inconsistent H&E coloration. 3.3 Conditional latent-diffusion model CPathOGen as shown in Figure 2 is built upon a latent diffusion model initialized from pretrained Stable Diffusion 2.1 weights [ 29 ] . We first adapt the pretrained visual prior to H&E tissue and subsequently introduce the structured spatial and morphology conditions. Let ℰ \mathcal{E} and 𝒟 \mathcal{D} denote the encoder and decoder of the pretrained variational autoencoder. An H&E tile x x is encoded as z 0 = ℰ ⁡ ( x ) , z_{0}=\mathcal{E}(x), (4) where z 0 z_{0} is its lower-dimensional latent representation.

The conditional denoising U-Net ϵ θ \epsilon_{\theta} predicts the added noise from the noisy latent, diffusion timestep, spatial condition, and morphology vector. It is optimized using ℒ diff = 𝔼 x , t , ϵ ​ [ ‖ ϵ − ϵ θ ​ ( z t , t , S , m ) ‖ 2 2 ] . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{diff}}=\mathbb{E}_{x,t,\epsilon}\left[\left\|\epsilon-\epsilon_{\theta}(z_{t},t;S,m)\right\|_{2}^{2}\right]. (6) The text condition is held fixed because synthesis is governed by the structured pathology controls rather than natural-language prompts. 3.4 Latent spatial conditioning The spatial condition is introduced through a trainable convolutional encoder E s E_{s} . Given the cellular map S ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] K × H × W S\in[0,1]^{K\times H\times W} , the encoder produces c s = E s ​ ( S ) , c s ∈ ℝ C s × h × w , c_{s}=E_{s}(S),\qquad c_{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{C_{s}\times h\times w}, (7) where C s C_{s} is the number of spatial feature channels and h × w h\times w is the spatial resolution of the diffusion latent. In our implementation, H = W = 512 H=W=512 , h = w = 64 h=w=64 , and C s = 4 C_{s}=4 . Let z t ∈ ℝ C z × h × w z_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{C_{z}\times h\times w} denote the noisy image latent at diffusion step t t , with C z = 4 C_{z}=4 . The encoded spatial features are concatenated with the noisy latent: z ~ t = [ z t ; λ s ​ c s ] ∈ ℝ ( C z + C s ) × h × w , \widetilde{z}_{t}=\left[z_{t};\lambda_{s}c_{s}\right]\in\mathbb{R}^{(C_{z}+C_{s})\times h\times w}, (8) where [ ⋅ ; ⋅ ] [\cdot;\cdot] denotes channel-wise concatenation and λ s \lambda_{s} controls the strength of spatial conditioning. The resulting tensor contains eight channels in our implementation.

The first U-Net convolution is expanded from four to eight input channels. The weights associated with the original latent channels retain their pretrained initialization, while the additional spatial-input weights are initialized to zero. The model can therefore begin from the pretrained H&E image prior and progressively learn how cell type, abundance, and location should affect synthesis. 3.5 Morphology and Stain modulation The global condition m m is injected throughout the denoising U-Net using feature-wise linear modulation. Let h ℓ ∈ ℝ B × C ℓ × h ℓ × w ℓ h_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times C_{\ell}\times h_{\ell}\times w_{\ell}} denote the output activation of residual block ℓ \ell , where B B is the batch size, C ℓ C_{\ell} is the number of channels, and h ℓ × w ℓ h_{\ell}\times w_{\ell} is the spatial resolution at that block. Each residual block has a learned two-layer mapping f ℓ : ℝ d → ℝ 2 ​ C ℓ , f_{\ell}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{2C_{\ell}}, which transforms the morphology vector into channel-wise scale and shift parameters: ( γ ℓ , β ℓ ) = f ℓ ​ ( m ) . (\gamma_{\ell},\beta_{\ell})=f_{\ell}(m). (9) Here, γ ℓ , β ℓ ∈ ℝ B × C ℓ \gamma_{\ell},\beta_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times C_{\ell}} are broadcast over the spatial dimensions of h ℓ h_{\ell} . The modulated activation is h ℓ ′ = ( 1 + γ ℓ ) ⊙ h ℓ + β ℓ , h^{\prime}_{\ell}=(1+\gamma_{\ell})\odot h_{\ell}+\beta_{\ell}, (10) where ⊙ \odot denotes channel-wise multiplication. The identity offset in 1 + γ ℓ 1+\gamma_{\ell} preserves the unmodulated block when the predicted scale is zero. Applying FiLM across the U-Net residual blocks allows nuclear geometry, texture, and appearance to influence multiple levels of the denoising hierarchy. The scale and shift parameters are bounded to prevent extreme conditioning values from overwhelming the learned image representation.

The spatial map and morphology vector consequently provide complementary controls: S S determines where cellular structures should occur, while m m controls their aggregate geometry and appearance. 3.6 Prediction-independent fidelity guidance Different diffusion seeds can vary in how faithfully they express the requested cellular arrangement. For each condition, we therefore generate a fixed set of candidate images and rank them according to agreement between the requested spatial map and the cellular organization recovered from each generated image. Let ℛ \mathcal{R} denote the candidate seed set and x r = G θ ​ ( S , m , ϵ r ) x_{r}=G_{\theta}(S,m,\epsilon_{r}) the image generated using seed r ∈ ℛ r\in\mathcal{R} . A cellular analyzer is applied to x r x_{r} , and a fidelity function Q ⁡ ( x r , S ) Q(x_{r},S) measures agreement between requested and recovered cell types and locations. The selected seed is r ⋆ = arg ⁡ max r ∈ ℛ ⁡ Q ⁡ ( x r , S ) . r^{\star}=\arg\max_{r\in\mathcal{R}}Q(x_{r},S). (11) CellViT++ supplies the primary agreement signal in our implementation. The fidelity function and candidate set are fixed before downstream evaluation, and selection does not observe the predictions, representations, or gradients of the model being probed. The selected image is then used for the corresponding counterfactual analysis. 3.7 Paired interventions and model probing At inference, users may edit an extracted condition or directly construct a custom spatial map and morphology vector. Let c = ( S , m ) c=(S,m) denote a baseline condition and ℐ j , δ \mathcal{I}_{j,\delta} an intervention of magnitude δ \delta applied to control family j j . A matched image pair is generated as x ( 0 ) = G θ ​ ( S , m , ϵ ) , x ( j , δ ) = G θ ​ ( ℐ j , δ ​ ( S , m ) , ϵ ) , x^{(0)}=G_{\theta}(S,m,\epsilon),\qquad x^{(j,\delta)}=G_{\theta}\left(\mathcal{I}_{j,\delta}(S,m),\epsilon\right), (12) where G θ G_{\theta} includes latent denoising and image decoding.

Both images reuse the same initial noise ϵ \epsilon , and all non-target conditioning variables remain fixed. For example, morphology interventions vary one nuclear property while preserving spatial organization and appearance. Spatial interventions modify cell composition, density, distance, or mixing while preserving the global morphology vector. Appearance interventions modify the selected color controls while preserving spatial and geometric conditions. Reusing the same noise reduces unrelated stochastic variation, although the requested intervention is subsequently verified from the generated image. For every intervention, CPathOGen records the source tile, conditioning variables, intervention magnitude, diffusion seed, generated image, and downstream output. These matched intervention records support model interpretation by revealing which controlled biological or appearance changes alter the model’s predictions or representations. 3.3 Conditional latent-diffusion model CPathOGen as shown in Figure 2 is built upon a latent diffusion model initialized from pretrained Stable Diffusion 2.1 weights [ 29 ] . These matched intervention records support model interpretation by revealing which controlled biological or appearance changes alter the model’s predictions or representations. 4 Experiments 4.1 Experimental setup We use 1,114 whole-slide images from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) Breast Cancer Cohort [ 34 ] . Slides are processed at 20 × 20\times magnification and divided into 512 × 512 512\times 512 H&E tiles. CellViT++ provides weak nucleus contours, centroids, and cell-type labels. Tiles containing more than two detected tumor cells are retained, yielding approximately 1.4 million tiles with aligned spatial maps and morphology/appearance vectors. Dataset partitions are separated at the patient level. CPathOGen is trained on eight NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPUs and evaluated using a fixed checkpoint. We use N R = 10,000 N_{R}=10{,}000 samples per distribution for realism and N = 1,000 N=1{,}000 baseline conditions for the remaining experiments. Morphology and appearance interventions use 𝒟 = { − 2 , − 1 , 0 , + 1 , + 2 } , \mathcal{D}=\{-2,-1,0,+1,+2\}, (14) where each value denotes the requested displacement from the baseline in training-set standard deviations. Thus, − 2 -2 and + 2 +2 represent two standard deviations below and above baseline, while 0 0 leaves the condition unchanged. Spatial experiments instead use ordered changes expressed directly in the cellular map.

ResNet-50 [ 13 ] , CTransPath, and UNI2-h are used as frozen feature extractors, and their tile embeddings are ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -normalized. For PAM50, patient- and class-balanced multinomial logistic regression heads are trained at the tile level under five patient-disjoint folds. Patient-level performance is obtained by averaging tile probabilities within each patient and is reported using macro one-vs-rest AUC. Counterfactual responses are measured directly between paired baseline and intervention tiles. Overall survival is evaluated using a fixed 16-tile bag for each patient. This common tile budget enables a consistent comparison between frozen embedding models and PathLUPI, a fully pretrained survival model designed natively for multi-tile input. For ResNet-50, CTransPath, and UNI2-h, tile embeddings are mean-pooled and ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -normalized before fitting a censor-aware Cox head. Each counterfactual replaces one tile in an otherwise unchanged bag. PathLUPI [ 19 ] receives the same 16 tiles but retains its released CONCH-based aggregation and survival formulation. Performance is measured using Harrell’s C-index, while counterfactual responses are calculated from predicted five-year survival probabilities. Generated images are never used for downstream-model training. 4.2 Distributional realism FID [ 15 ] and KID [ 5 ] compare N R N_{R} generated images with an independent reference set of N R N_{R} real tiles. Generation conditions are obtained from a separate, non-overlapping set of real tiles, ensuring that the conditioning and reference distributions contain no shared images. The unfiltered setting uses one generation per condition, whereas the selected setting applies the eight-candidate spatial selection procedure from Sec. 3 . Total-count fidelity is the Spearman correlation between requested and recovered cellular burden over N N conditions. Perimeter remains part of the conditioning vector but is omitted because of its strong relationship with area. athOGen interventions and one generator-independent nuisance control. Stain brightness jointly modifies RGB appearance. Nuclear enlargement changes nuclear area and perimeter, while shape irregularity changes eccentricity and reduces solidity while preserving nuclear area. Immune burden changes inflammatory-cell abundance, and tumor–immune mixing relocates immune cells from mixed to segregated configurations without changing tumor or immune counts. Image rotation applies 0 ∘ 0^{\circ} , 90 ∘ 90^{\circ} , 180 ∘ 180^{\circ} , and 270 ∘ 270^{\circ} transformations to the same generated reference tile. We group nuclear enlargement, shape irregularity, immune burden, and tumor–immune mixing into the biological intervention set ℬ \mathcal{B} , reflecting nuclear phenotype and tumor-microenvironment organization [ 44 , 39 ] . Stain brightness and image rotation form the nuisance set 𝒰 \mathcal{U} , representing appearance and orientation changes that should not independently determine the biological endpoint [ 33 ] . These groups define the Biology-to-Nuisance Ratio and do not imply biological causality. Supplementary material presents representative images from the five CPathOGen interventions. For model f f , let 𝐩 f ​ ( x i ) \mathbf{p}_{f}(x_{i}) and 𝐩 f ​ ( x i , e , δ ) \mathbf{p}_{f}(x_{i,e,\delta}) denote the output distributions for baseline i i and experiment e e at level δ \delta . Total variation distance is d i , e , δ = 1 2 ​ ‖ 𝐩 f ​ ( x i , e , δ ) − 𝐩 f ​ ( x i ) ‖ 1 . d_{i,e,\delta}=\frac{1}{2}\left\|\mathbf{p}_{f}(x_{i,e,\delta})-\mathbf{p}_{f}(x_{i})\right\|_{1}. (15) For PAM50, 𝐩 f \mathbf{p}_{f} is the four-class subtype distribution. For survival, it is the Bernoulli distribution formed from the model’s survival probability. Prediction-flip rate records a change in the PAM50 argmax class or crossing the 0.5 0.5 survival-probability threshold.

D_{f}(e)=\frac{1}{N|\mathcal{D}_{e}|}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{\delta\in\mathcal{D}_{e}}d_{i,e,\delta}. (16) The Biology-to-Nuisance Ratio is BNR ⁡ ( f ) = | ℬ | − 1 ​ ∑ e ∈ ℬ D f ​ ( e ) | 𝒰 | − 1 ​ ∑ e ∈ 𝒰 D f ​ ( e ) . \mathrm{BNR}(f)=\frac{|\mathcal{B}|^{-1}\sum_{e\in\mathcal{B}}D_{f}(e)}{|\mathcal{U}|^{-1}\sum_{e\in\mathcal{U}}D_{f}(e)}. (17) BNR above one indicates a larger average response to the evaluated biological interventions than to the stain and rotation nuisance controls. It measures relative sensitivity, not predictive performance or biological correctness. UNI2-h achieves the strongest PAM50 discrimination, but it is not the least sensitive model, demonstrating that predictive performance and counterfactual stability capture distinct properties. The dominant biological intervention varies across encoders: shape irregularity produces the largest response for ResNet-50, immune burden for CTransPath, and nuclear enlargement for UNI2-h. Tumor–immune mixing produces the smallest biological response across all three encoders. Rotation generally causes less output movement than stain brightness, although its nonzero flip rates reveal residual orientation sensitivity. Survival effects are attenuated because each intervention replaces only one tile within a fixed 16-tile patient representation. Immune burden nevertheless produces the largest response for every survival model. PathLUPI achieves a lower C-index than the task-trained CTransPath and UNI2-h models but the highest BNR, driven primarily by its response to immune burden. Given that PathLUPI is used without cohort-specific training, this suggests that its released survival representation preferentially captures immune-related variation, although the higher BNR does not compensate for lower predictive discrimination.

Patient-clustered 95% confidence intervals remain above one for every model and task, supporting greater average sensitivity to the evaluated biological interventions than to stain brightness and image rotation. 4.1 Experimental setup We use 1,114 whole-slide images from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) Breast Cancer Cohort [ 34 ] . Slides are processed at 20 × 20\times magnification and divided into 512 × 512 512\times 512 H&E tiles. CellViT++ provides weak nucleus contours, centroids, and cell-type labels. Tiles containing more than two detected tumor cells are retained, yielding approximately 1.4 million tiles with aligned spatial maps and morphology/appearance vectors. Dataset partitions are separated at the patient level. CPathOGen is trained on eight NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPUs and evaluated using a fixed checkpoint. We use N R = 10,000 N_{R}=10{,}000 samples per distribution for realism and N = 1,000 N=1{,}000 baseline conditions for the remaining experiments. Morphology and appearance interventions use 𝒟 = { − 2 , − 1 , 0 , + 1 , + 2 } , \mathcal{D}=\{-2,-1,0,+1,+2\}, (14) where each value denotes the requested displacement from the baseline in training-set standard deviations. Thus, − 2 -2 and + 2 +2 represent two standard deviations below and above baseline, while 0 0 leaves the condition unchanged. Spatial experiments instead use ordered changes expressed directly in the cellular map. ResNet-50 [ 13 ] , CTransPath, and UNI2-h are used as frozen feature extractors, and their tile embeddings are ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -normalized. For PAM50, patient- and class-balanced multinomial logistic regression heads are trained at the tile level under five patient-disjoint folds. Patient-level performance is obtained by averaging tile probabilities within each patient and is reported using macro one-vs-rest AUC. Counterfactual responses are measured directly between paired baseline and intervention tiles. Overall survival is evaluated using a fixed 16-tile bag for each patient.

This common tile budget enables a consistent comparison between frozen embedding models and PathLUPI, a fully pretrained survival model designed natively for multi-tile input. For ResNet-50, CTransPath, and UNI2-h, tile embeddings are mean-pooled and ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -normalized before fitting a censor-aware Cox head. Each counterfactual replaces one tile in an otherwise unchanged bag. PathLUPI [ 19 ] receives the same 16 tiles but retains its released CONCH-based aggregation and survival formulation. Performance is measured using Harrell’s C-index, while counterfactual responses are calculated from predicted five-year survival probabilities. Generated images are never used for downstream-model training. 4.5 Counterfactual model probing We evaluate five CPathOGen interventions and one generator-independent nuisance control. Stain brightness jointly modifies RGB appearance. Nuclear enlargement changes nuclear area and perimeter, while shape irregularity changes eccentricity and reduces solidity while preserving nuclear area. Immune burden changes inflammatory-cell abundance, and tumor–immune mixing relocates immune cells from mixed to segregated configurations without changing tumor or immune counts. Image rotation applies 0 ∘ 0^{\circ} , 90 ∘ 90^{\circ} , 180 ∘ 180^{\circ} , and 270 ∘ 270^{\circ} transformations to the same generated reference tile. We group nuclear enlargement, shape irregularity, immune burden, and tumor–immune mixing into the biological intervention set ℬ \mathcal{B} , reflecting nuclear phenotype and tumor-microenvironment organization [ 44 , 39 ] . Stain brightness and image rotation form the nuisance set 𝒰 \mathcal{U} , representing appearance and orientation changes that should not independently determine the biological endpoint [ 33 ] . These groups define the Biology-to-Nuisance Ratio and do not imply biological causality. Supplementary material presents representative images from the five CPathOGen interventions.

It measures relative sensitivity, not predictive performance or biological correctness. UNI2-h achieves the strongest PAM50 discrimination, but it is not the least sensitive model, demonstrating that predictive performance and counterfactual stability capture distinct properties. The dominant biological intervention varies across encoders: shape irregularity produces the largest response for ResNet-50, immune burden for CTransPath, and nuclear enlargement for UNI2-h. Tumor–immune mixing produces the smallest biological response across all three encoders.

Rotation generally causes less output movement than stain brightness, although its nonzero flip rates reveal residual orientation sensitivity. Survival effects are attenuated because each intervention replaces only one tile within a fixed 16-tile patient representation. Immune burden nevertheless produces the largest response for every survival model. PathLUPI achieves a lower C-index than the task-trained CTransPath and UNI2-h models but the highest BNR, driven primarily by its response to immune burden. Given that PathLUPI is used without cohort-specific training, this suggests that its released survival representation preferentially captures immune-related variation, although the higher BNR does not compensate for lower predictive discrimination. Patient-clustered 95% confidence intervals remain above one for every model and task, supporting greater average sensitivity to the evaluated biological interventions than to stain brightness and image rotation. 5 Conclusion CPathOGen provides a structured framework for generating spatially and morphologically controlled H&E counterfactuals and using them to audit computational pathology models. The fidelity experiments show that requested cellular organization and appearance changes can be recovered across independent analyzers, while downstream probing reveals that predictive performance and intervention sensitivity describe different model properties. This enables safety-oriented evaluation beyond conventional accuracy: models can be examined for sensitivity to biologically motivated factors, robustness to nuisance variation, and potential reliance on spurious signals such as stain or orientation. Such evidence may help identify models requiring additional augmentation or refinement and support model selection based on both performance and feature reliance.

The framework nevertheless requires a large, representative training corpus with sufficiently reliable cellular annotations or weak labels, and its counterfactuals remain condition-matched synthetic samples rather than exact reconstructions. Unmodeled properties may change, and observed prediction shifts characterize model behavior under synthetic interventions rather than patient-level biological causality. Future work should include external-cohort and expert validation, richer cellular conditions, and more efficient candidate selection. More broadly, the same controlled-generation and paired-probing formulation could be adapted to other imaging fields in which spatial organization and global attributes jointly influence model predictions.
